title: SYSK Selects: How Mirrors Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the 2010 episode "How Mirrors Work." Chuck introduces it as his pick. The hosts cover mirror history from polished obsidian (Anatolia, about 6000 BC) through polished metal, glass mirrors with Venetian trade secrets, and Justus von Liebig's 1835 silvering process. They discuss mirrors' role in self-portraits and linear perspective, reflecting telescopes, and the Archimedes death-ray legend. The physics section covers the law of reflection, specular versus diffuse reflection, virtual images, the Venus effect, and left-right reversal. Other topics are concave and convex mirrors, non-reversing mirrors, two-way mirrors, movie mirror scenes, mirror superstitions and folklore, and a listener mail plea for a New York City Walk to Beat Lung Cancer.

segments.title: Selects introduction and opening banter
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the episode as his Selects pick from September 2010. The hosts chat about childhood mirror habits and body image.

segments.title: History of mirrors
segments.summary: Mirrors began as polished obsidian in Anatolia around 6000 BC, then moved to heavy polished silver, bronze, and copper that limited size and were costly. Glass mirrors improved with Venetian production. Liebig's 1835 silvering process produced the modern mirror.

segments.title: Mirrors, art, and science
segments.summary: Good mirrors enabled self-portraits and coincided with the adoption of linear perspective in art. Mirrors also inspired reflecting telescopes. The hosts discuss the Archimedes death-ray legend and MythBusters' test of it.

segments.title: Law of reflection and light physics
segments.summary: Chuck explains the law of reflection, with the angle of incidence equal to the angle of reflection, using sunsets and glare as examples. The hosts contrast diffuse reflection from hands with specular reflection from mirrors, which produces a virtual image.

segments.title: Venus effect and left-right reversal
segments.summary: The Venus effect describes paintings of Venus holding a mirror while the viewer, not Venus, sees her face. The hosts explain that mirrors reverse front and back, not left and right, using a virtual-image distance argument.

segments.title: Concave, convex, non-reversing and two-way mirrors
segments.summary: Concave mirrors project real images, as in holograms, and are used to light the Olympic torch. Convex mirrors widen the view, as on car passenger mirrors. Two perpendicular mirrors give a non-reversing view, and a patent was held by John Derby. Two-way mirrors reflect on the lit side and show the dark room when lighting is unbalanced.

segments.title: Mirrors in film and folklore
segments.summary: The hosts discuss movie mirror tropes such as the medicine cabinet scare and the Poltergeist scene. They also cover mirror superstitions: broken mirrors and seven-year bad luck, Bloody Mary, covering mirrors after a Jewish death, New Year's Eve mirror rituals, and Chinese mirror-people folklore.

segments.title: Listener mail: Walk to Beat Lung Cancer
segments.summary: A listener named John promotes the New York City Walk to Beat Lung Cancer in Battery Park in October 2010, which is organized by Jess, and gives website and social media details.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and direct listeners to howstuffworks.com.
